title: Metabolic and Nutritional Science Overview
intro: An interactive deep dive into three powerful metabolic interventions: methionine restriction, intermittent fasting, and sulforaphane. Each section expands with detailed mechanisms, clinical evidence, and safety notes.

sections.title: Robert M. Hoffman: Methionine Addiction
sections.content: Robert M. Hoffman has extensively documented 'methionine addiction'—a fundamental hallmark of cancer cells often termed the Hoffman Effect. Unlike normal cells, many cancer cells cannot thrive without exogenous methionine, despite an internal capacity for synthesis. This vulnerability is exploited via methionine restriction (MR) using diet or recombinant methioninase (rMETase).

bullets.title: Selective Inhibition
bullets.text: Methionine restriction selectively arrests cancer cells in the S/G2 phase of the cell cycle while sparing normal cells. This phase‑specific arrest provides a therapeutic window, as normal tissues remain largely unaffected.

bullets.title: Therapeutic Window
bullets.text: Continuous MR is essential; cancer cells may resume proliferation upon methionine replenishment. In vivo models show that intermittent restriction fails to sustain tumour stasis, highlighting the need for steady‑state methionine depletion.

bullets.title: Methodology
bullets.text: Recombinant methioninase (rMETase) directly degrades serum methionine, creating a rapid methionine‑depletion catastrophe in tumours while normal cells utilise endogenous synthesis. Oral formulations and PEGylated versions are under development for clinical use.

sections.title: Intermittent Fasting (12/12 & 16/8)
sections.content: Intermittent fasting (IF), especially Time‑Restricted Eating (TRE) protocols like 16:8 and 12:12, is one of the most studied dietary strategies for metabolic health. These protocols facilitate a natural 'metabolic switch' from glucose to fat oxidation and ketone body production during the fasting window.

bullets.title: Mechanisms
bullets.text: During the fasting period, insulin levels drop, AMPK is activated, and mTOR signalling is suppressed. This triggers autophagy—a cellular repair and recycling process—while promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and reduced oxidative stress.

bullets.title: Benefits
bullets.text: Clinical evidence shows improvements in weight management, insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and inflammatory markers. Time‑restricted eating also improves circadian rhythm alignment, which independently enhances metabolic outcomes.

bullets.title: Safety Protocols
bullets.text: Systematic reviews confirm that 16:8 and 12:12 protocols are safe and well‑tolerated. Proper implementation preserves lean muscle mass, and adherence is superior to many calorie‑restriction diets. However, medical supervision is advised for individuals on glucose‑lowering medications.

sections.title: Sulforaphane Studies
sections.content: Sulforaphane, an isothiocyanate derived from cruciferous vegetables (especially broccoli sprouts), is a potent activator of the cytoprotective Nrf2 pathway. It has attracted intense research for its ability to strengthen cellular defence against oxidative stress and chronic inflammation.

bullets.title: Mechanisms
bullets.text: Sulforaphane covalently modifies Keap1, allowing Nrf2 to translocate to the nucleus and upregulate over 200 antioxidant and detoxification genes. This hormetic effect also inhibits NF‑κB, reducing systemic inflammation.

bullets.title: Therapeutic Potential
bullets.text: Human trials demonstrate benefits in neurodegenerative conditions, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. It is remarkably safe, with low toxicity even at high doses. In autism spectrum disorder, sulforaphane improved social interaction and behaviour scores.

bullets.title: Bioavailability
bullets.text: The conversion of glucoraphanin to active sulforaphane requires myrosinase, an enzyme destroyed by cooking. Fresh raw sprouts or properly processed supplements containing active myrosinase are far more effective than heat‑treated preparations.
